meta.titre: Electromagnetism: electromagnets, magnetic force and the motor
meta.sous_theme: Magnetic effect of a current, electromagnets and Fleming's left-hand rule

sections.contenu_markdown: At a scrapyard in Douala, a crane lifts old cars with a huge magnet that is switched on to pick the metal up and switched off to drop it. The same principle makes an electric bell ring, a relay switch a large current, a loudspeaker produce sound and a motor turn a fan. All use the fact that a current produces a magnetic field and that a current in a magnetic field feels a force. At the GCE you are asked to explain electromagnets, to choose between soft and hard magnetic materials, and to apply Fleming's left-hand rule.

items: A magnet has two poles; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
A magnetic field is the region in which a magnet or a magnetic material feels a force.
Current is the flow of charge; conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal.

sections.titre: Magnetic effect of a current and the force on a conductor
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Magnetic field of a current.** A straight wire carrying a current has circular magnetic field lines around it. Right-hand grip rule: point the thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field. A **solenoid** (a long coil) has a field like a bar magnet. Viewed from one end, if the current goes round clockwise that end is a south pole; if it goes round anticlockwise that end is a north pole.

**Electromagnet.** A solenoid wound on a soft iron core. Its strength increases with: (i) a larger current, (ii) more turns of wire, (iii) a soft iron core. It can be switched on and off, and its strength and polarity can be changed by changing the current.

**Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (the motor effect).** A wire carrying a current and placed at right angles to a magnetic field feels a force at right angles to both the wire and the field. The force is larger for a bigger current, a stronger field and a longer length of wire in the field. It reverses if either the current or the field is reversed (but not if both are). It is zero if the wire is parallel to the field.

**Fleming's left-hand rule.** Stretch the thumb, the first finger and the second finger of the left hand at right angles to each other: the thumb gives the direction of the **force** (motion), the first finger gives the direction of the **field** (north to south), and the second finger gives the direction of the **current** (conventional current).

| Material | Behaviour | Uses |
|---|---|---|
| Soft magnetic (iron) | magnetised and demagnetised easily | electromagnets, relays, electric bells, transformer cores |
| Hard magnetic (steel) | keeps its magnetism | permanent magnets, compass needles, loudspeaker magnets |

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked why soft iron is used or how a device works
variantes.contenu_markdown: Soft iron is used for the core of an electromagnet because it is magnetised quickly when the current flows and loses its magnetism when the current stops. Steel would stay magnetised and could not release the load. In an electric bell, the electromagnet attracts a soft iron armature that strikes the gong and, at the same time, breaks the circuit. The magnet then releases the armature and the circuit is remade, so the process repeats. In a relay, a small current in the coil of an electromagnet closes the contacts of a circuit that carries a much larger current.

variantes.nom: Force on a wire: using the left-hand rule
variantes.quand_utiliser: when the directions of the current and of the field are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Place the first finger along the field and the second along the conventional current, with the thumb at right angles to both. The thumb shows the force. If the current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of the supply, use this as the direction of the second finger. Reversing the current or the field reverses the force. The same rule applies to a coil or to the side of a loop.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked to explain how a motor turns, or how to make it faster
variantes.contenu_markdown: A rectangular coil lies between the poles of a magnet. The currents in the two long sides of the coil flow in opposite directions, so the forces on them are opposite and the coil turns. A **split-ring commutator** reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the forces always turn the coil in the same direction; carbon brushes press on the commutator and connect it to the supply. The motor turns faster or with a larger turning effect when the current is increased, a stronger magnet is used, or the coil has more turns.

sections.enonce_markdown: A straight horizontal wire runs from west to east between two magnets which produce a magnetic field directed vertically downwards. The conventional current in the wire flows from west to east and the force on the wire is $0.60\,\mathrm{N}$. (a) State the direction of the force on the wire. (b) What is the force if the current is doubled? (c) What is the direction of the force if the field is reversed? (d) The current is doubled and the field is halved. What is the force?

etapes.justification: Fleming's left-hand rule needs the field (first finger) and the current (second finger).
etapes.resultat_markdown: First finger: vertically downwards. Second finger: towards the east.

etapes.action: Apply the rule to find the direction of the force.
etapes.justification: The thumb is at right angles to both fingers and gives the force (thumb: **motion**).
The force is proportional to the current, so doubling the current doubles the force; the direction is unchanged.
Reversing the field or the current reverses the force.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The force is now towards the **south**.

etapes.action: Double the current and halve the field.
etapes.justification: Force is proportional to current $\times$ field, so the two changes cancel.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The force is $0.60\,\mathrm{N}$ towards the north. It doubles to $1.2\,\mathrm{N}$ when the current doubles, reverses to the south when the field is reversed, and returns to $0.60\,\mathrm{N}$ when the current is doubled and the field halved.

items.erreur_markdown: Steel is the best core for an electromagnet because it makes the strongest magnet.
items.pourquoi_faux: Steel keeps its magnetism after the current is switched off, so the electromagnet could not release its load or be reversed. Soft iron loses its magnetism almost completely.
items.correction_markdown: Use soft iron for the core; use steel for permanent magnets.

items.erreur_markdown: The force on a current-carrying wire is in the same direction as the magnetic field.
items.pourquoi_faux: The force is at right angles to both the field and the wire. A force along the field would be an error: the thumb, the first finger and the second finger point in three perpendicular directions.
items.correction_markdown: Apply the left-hand rule with three perpendicular directions.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the right hand for the force on a wire in a motor.
items.pourquoi_faux: The left hand is used for motors (the force produced by a current). The right-hand rule is used for generators.
items.correction_markdown: Left-hand rule for the motor effect (current gives motion); right-hand rule for induction (motion gives current).

items.erreur_markdown: Reversing both the current and the magnetic field reverses the force.
items.pourquoi_faux: Each reversal alone would reverse the force, so doing both gives back the original direction.
items.correction_markdown: Count the number of reversals: an odd number reverses the force, an even number keeps it.

items.erreur_markdown: A motor needs no commutator because the current is always in the same direction.
items.pourquoi_faux: After half a turn the side of the coil that was near the north pole is now near the south pole, so without a commutator the force would turn the coil back. The commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn.
items.correction_markdown: The split-ring commutator keeps the coil turning in one direction.

items.enonce_markdown: State three ways of increasing the strength of an electromagnet. A current flows anticlockwise round a solenoid when it is viewed from the left-hand end. State the polarity of that end.
items.solution_markdown:
The strength increases if (i) **the current is increased**, (ii) **the number of turns is increased**, (iii) **a soft iron core is inserted** (or a larger core is used).

Anticlockwise current when viewed from an end makes that end a **north pole**.

items.enonce_markdown: A horizontal wire carries a current towards the north in a magnetic field directed vertically upwards. (a) State the direction of the force on the wire. (b) What happens to the direction of the force if both the current and the field are reversed? (c) The current in the wire is zero. What is the force? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Second finger (current) towards the north and first finger (field) upwards; the thumb points **east**, so the force is towards the east.

(b) Reversing both leaves the direction **unchanged** (towards the east), because each reversal reverses the force and the two cancel.

(c) The force is **zero**: a force acts only on a moving charge, so with no current there is no force on the wire.

items.enonce_markdown: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between two magnets. (a) Explain why the coil starts to turn when a current flows. (b) What is the function of the split-ring commutator? (c) The current is $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ and the force on each long side of the coil is $0.80\,\mathrm{N}$. Find the force on each side if the current is raised to $3.0\,\mathrm{A}$ and state two other changes that would make the motor turn faster.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The currents in the two long sides of the coil flow in opposite directions. By Fleming's left-hand rule, the force on one side is upwards and on the other side downwards. These two forces make a turning effect, so the coil rotates.

(b) The commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the force on each side always pushes it the same way round and the rotation continues in one direction.

(c) Force is proportional to the current: $0.80 \times \dfrac{3.0}{2.0}$, so **$1.2\,\mathrm{N}$** on each side. Two other changes: **use a stronger magnet** and **use more turns on the coil**.

items_markdown: A current produces a **magnetic field**: circles round a wire (right-hand grip rule); a solenoid behaves like a bar magnet.
An **electromagnet** is a coil on a soft iron core; it is stronger with more current and more turns, and it can be switched off.
**Soft iron** (magnetised and demagnetised easily) is used for electromagnets, relays and bells; **steel** keeps its magnetism and is used for permanent magnets.
A current in a magnetic field feels a **force**; **Fleming's left-hand rule**: thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current, all at right angles.
A d.c. motor uses a coil, a magnet and a split-ring commutator; it turns faster with more current, a stronger magnet or more turns.
